summary:
We developed "Earth → Moon → Earth," an interactive 3D cinematic simulation of a rocket journey to the Moon and back, built with Three.js and WebGL. It shows the full mission: launch from the pad, first-stage separation, transit to the Moon, lunar orbit, return, service module separation, atmospheric re-entry with a heat shield, and landing on an aircraft carrier at sea. The capsule design is inspired by NASA's Orion, and the mission sequence follows Apollo and Artemis, using NASA data such as Earth–Moon distance, planetary radii, trip duration, and re-entry speed.

The project addresses the challenge by turning complex spaceflight stages into a clear, visual experience. Users get an Arabic interface with a timeline, speed control, and a Director Mode to move the camera and record video, all in the browser on mobile or desktop.

It matters because space education is often theoretical and scarce in Arabic. Our tool makes space missions easier to understand and inspires students toward STEM.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

"Earth → Moon → Earth" is an interactive 3D cinematic simulation that runs in any web browser. It follows a two-stage rocket through the full mission: launch from the pad, first-stage separation, transit through space, orbit around the Moon, return to Earth, service module separation, atmospheric re-entry with a heat shield, and a final landing on an aircraft carrier at sea. Users can play or pause the journey, drag a timeline to any moment, change speed (0.5x, 1x, 2x), and read a short caption explaining each phase. A Director Mode lets users move the camera freely, adjust the lens, save custom camera paths, and record video directly from the browser.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Spaceflight stages are usually taught with text and static images, which makes them hard to picture. Our project lets anyone see the whole mission in a few minutes, with no scientific background and no installation. It has an Arabic right-to-left interface, helping fill the gap in interactive Arabic space-education content. We hope it encourages students to take an interest in space science and STEM, and teachers can use it in class or to create their own mission videos.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D rendering

- JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for logic, controls, and interface

- GLB and FBX 3D models for the rocket and first stage

- Procedural textures and custom shaders for the Earth, Moon, atmosphere glow, stars, and engine flames

- Noto Kufi Arabic font for the Arabic interface

- The MediaRecorder browser feature for video recording

NASA DATA USED

We used NASA figures such as the average Earth–Moon distance (about 384,400 km), Earth and Moon radii, the outbound trip duration of about 3 days, and a re-entry speed of about 11 km/s. The mission sequence follows Apollo and Artemis, and the capsule, service module, and heat shield are inspired by NASA's Orion.

CREATIVITY

We combined education with filmmaking. Instead of a fixed animation, we built a cinematic experience that users can direct themselves. The journey also ends with a modern recovery at sea on an aircraft carrier, which makes the ending easy to visualize.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accessibility: it works on mobile and desktop with no installation.

- Language: a full Arabic interface for Arabic-speaking learners.

- Accuracy and honesty: the simulation follows real mission phases and NASA data, but sizes and distances are not to real scale. We state this clearly on screen, since it is a conceptual demonstration and not a physics simulation.

- Performance: optimized models and textures so it runs smoothly on regular devices.
